about:
A PROJECT-DEFINED EDITORIAL EQUIVALENT, NOT AN EXTERNAL SYLLABUS. NOTHING IN THIS FILE MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO ANY MALAYALAM EXAMINING OR LANGUAGE BODY. core/exam-levels.json records malayalam as exam 'no widely-sat ladder', basis 'editorial', and it carries NO caveat -- so unlike Tamil, whose entry names its diglossia, this track hands the inventory no external steer at all. Kerala's state school syllabi and the Kerala Sahitya Akademi exist, but they are built for children schooled in Malayalam or for literary attainment rather than for an adult second-language learner against CEFR can-do descriptors, and neither was consulted. Read 'A1' here as the CEFR descriptor -- can greet, introduce oneself, and handle a short exchange in everyday spoken Malayalam -- and as a measuring stick this project built for itself.

EXAM ENVELOPE: NONE EXISTS. There is no malayalam/task-shapes/ and no malayalam/mocks/, and no malayalam/assessment.json. So unlike Hindi and Marathi, whose inventories could mine a checked-in mock for the exponent a paper item actually needs, nothing here can say which task demands which word. Where those files write 'the mock asks for X', this one can only write 'an A1 learner needs X'. That is a weaker claim and is stated as one.

SEARCH FOR AN EXTERNAL SOURCE: NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION. The project settled at HL-C287/HL-C290 that the proxy derivation is the method for tracks with no sat ladder, and the search was deliberately not redone for Malayalam. Saying so is what keeps 'we did not look' from reading as 'there is nothing to find'.

THE REGISTER COLUMN IS MEASURED, NOT BORROWED. Tamil's inventory carries a register column because core/exam-levels.json names Tamil's diglossia in a caveat. Malayalam has no caveat, so this file measured the corpus instead of importing Tamil's shape. What it found is a DIFFERENT axis: four lessons carry register 'formal' and every one is a Sanskrit-tatsama time-of-day greeting, two carry 'literary'/'literary-narrative' and both teach a native word the everyday Sanskrit one displaced, and one teaches respect as grammatical plurality. That is a lexical borrowed-against-inherited split plus an honorific, and this file claims exactly that and does not claim a literary/spoken diglossia. The eighteen lessons carrying variety 'standard' rather than 'standard-colloquial' were checked and are ALL writing lessons, so they are an artefact of the script runway and not evidence of a second variety.
source: PROJECT-DEFINED. LEVEL PROXY: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, the DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Its own source is the Instituto Cervantes Plan Curricular inventories. The proxy supplies the LEVEL and the shape of the columns; every Malayalam exponent is this project's choice, and every point records which Spanish point or points it was derived from.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json
anchors.note: The DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Spanish is a proxy for LEVEL, never for grammar: each point was read as 'what must an A1 learner be able to do here', and the Malayalam exponent that carries the same load was then chosen. Where Malayalam carries the load with machinery Spanish does not have -- case suffixes, a dative subject, a question particle, a verb that never agrees -- the point is restated around the Malayalam machinery and its Spanish origin recorded in derivedFrom.

anchors.title: Council of Europe, CEFR Companion Volume
anchors.note: Supplies the meaning of 'A1' as a can-do band. It describes what a learner can DO and names no language's forms, which is exactly why a second, language-shaped source was needed and why the Spanish inventory is used as the proxy for that shape.

anchors.title: malayalam/lessons/ as merged on main
anchors.note: 292 lessons, all schema_version 2, introducing 358 atoms. Every probe in this file names an atom drawn from this set and was checked mechanically against it before the file was written; no probe names an id that a future lesson is expected to introduce.

anchors.title: this project's judgement about Malayalam
anchors.note: Where a Spanish point has no single Malayalam exponent, the choice of which Malayalam form carries the load is this project's and is defended in the point's own note. The clearest cases are the dative subject standing in for gustar, undu standing in for both hay and tener, and the -o particle standing in for Spanish interrogative inversion.

communicative-functions.source: Derived from the PCIC functional inventory by way of core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json.
communicative-functions.note: The Spanish functional subsections were walked in full and each was answered with the Malayalam exponent that carries it. Partial because the answers are this project's editorial choices rather than an examining body's list, and because no Malayalam mock exists to check them against.

grammar.source: Derived from the PCIC grammar inventory by way of core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json.
grammar.note: Every Spanish A1 grammar category was answered, including the ones whose Malayalam answer is that the category does not exist. Partial because a Malayalam-shaped grammar inventory would enumerate categories Spanish never raises -- the full case series, the relative participle, the quotative -- and this file reaches those only where a Spanish point happened to point at them.

phonology-orthography.source: Derived from the PCIC orthography inventory, plus this track's own script lessons.
phonology-orthography.note: The script column is measured against the corpus rather than against Malayalam: 67 distinct characters appear in headwords and 58 are taught. Partial for two reasons -- the nine untaught characters, and the fact that the pronunciation points are answered by SHAPE lessons rather than by sound lessons, which is honest and thin.

lexicon.source: Derived from the PCIC notional inventories by way of core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json.
lexicon.note: All twenty Spanish specific-notion areas were walked. Seven of them -- leisure, media, money and shopping, services, medicine, the arts, technology -- have no Malayalam word in the corpus at all, and are enumerated as uncovered rather than omitted.

probeSemantics: A probe is the set of atoms whose presence in the corpus demonstrates the point. ALL of them must be introduced for the point to count: a point covered by half its atoms is not covered, because a candidate asked for the whole of something does not get partial credit for half of it. probe: null means nothing in the corpus corresponds to the point, and every null carries a note naming what is missing -- those notes are a work queue and are written as one.

points.label: proper nouns: a personal name, given in an introduction and used in address
points.note: peru and both halves of the frame are chapter 2, and the frame is what an introduction actually uses.

points.label: place names: the town you live in, and the country you are from
points.note: naadu ('home country', ML-C55-homeland) is the nearest thing taught, and it names a KIND of place rather than one. No settlement name, no name of Kerala or of India, appears anywhere in 292 lessons -- so a learner can answer 'where are you from' only with a category. One lesson teaching uuru ('town') plus Keralam would close this and ML-A1-NG3-07 together.

points.label: common nouns naming stretches of time
points.note: divasam (day), mani (hour) and the four kaalangal (seasons) between them cover the day, the hour and the year.

points.label: Malayalam has no grammatical gender on the noun, and the noun therefore never agrees
points.note: The Spanish points ask what a learner must handle about gender agreement. In Malayalam the honest answer is that there is none to handle: ML-C05-samsaarikkuka states that the verb never agrees with anything, which is the same fact seen from the verb's end. Restated around the Malayalam machinery rather than dropped.

points.label: natural gender by separate words: makan against makal, achhan against amma
points.note: Where Spanish has padre/madre, Malayalam has the same heteronymy: makan/makal and the six kudumbam words.

points.label: number: the plural suffix -kal and when a bare noun already reads as plural
points.note: The plural is never taught. -kal appears inside taught headwords -- nirangal (colours), maasangal (months), shareera-bhaagangal (body parts), kaalangal (seasons) -- so the learner has met the suffix four times as part of a word and has never been told it is a suffix. That is the cheapest grammar lesson available to this track.

points.label: qualifying adjectives used before a noun
points.note: valiya, cheriya and nalla, plus the rule that ties them together.

points.label: the adjective is invariable: it never changes for gender, number or case
points.note: ML-C42-adjective-system teaches exactly this -- 'before the noun, unchanged'. Two Spanish points about agreement collapse into one Malayalam point about its absence.

points.label: position: the adjective stands before its noun, always
points.note: The mirror image of the Spanish point, and the reason it is worth stating: Spanish puts it after, Malayalam before, and neither language allows the other order.

points.label: relational adjectives: naming where a person or thing is from
points.note: No gentilic is taught. There is no word for 'Indian', 'Keralite' or 'Malayali' anywhere, which is the same hole as ML-A1-N-02 seen from the adjective's side.

points.label: degree: intensifying an adjective
points.note: valare ('very') is not taught, and neither is any other degree word. The track teaches five adjectives and no way to grade any of them, so 'good' cannot become 'very good'. Three Spanish points land on this one gap.

points.label: age as a quality: old and new of a thing
points.note: puthiya and pazhaya are taught, and the lesson is explicit that pazhaya is used of a thing and not of a person. Age of a PERSON is ML-A1-TIME-08.

points.category: Nirdeshakam (definiteness, and the article Malayalam does not have)
points.label: Malayalam has no definite article: a bare noun is definite or indefinite by context
points.note: The Spanish question is 'how does a learner mark definiteness'. Malayalam's answer is that it does not mark it at all, and reaches for ith/ath when it must. Restated around the Malayalam machinery.

points.category: Nirdeshakam (definiteness, and the article Malayalam does not have)
points.label: the indefinite: oru before a noun
points.note: oru ('a, one') is never taught, although onnu ('one') is. That is a one-word lesson which would let every noun in chapters 46 to 66 be asked for singly.

points.category: Nirdeshakam (definiteness, and the article Malayalam does not have)
points.label: no article contractions exist, because there is no article to contract
points.note: Recorded so the walk is total. Nothing in Malayalam corresponds and nothing needs teaching; the point is enumerated rather than dropped because a reader comparing the two inventories should see it answered.

points.label: the i- / a- / e- system: this, that, and the question word, built on one pattern
points.note: Malayalam does in one three-way prefix what Spanish does with este/ese/aquel plus separate interrogatives: i- is near, a- is far, e- asks. ML-C41-deixis-system teaches the pattern itself, which is why one point carries two Spanish ones.

points.label: ith and ath: this one and that one
ivide and avide: here and there
points.note: Spanish needs three (aqui, ahi, alli); Malayalam's taught set is two, and the third degree is not taught.

points.label: position: the demonstrative stands before its noun and cannot follow it
first person: njaan, and the fact that Malayalam cannot drop it
points.note: The point where Malayalam and Spanish are exact opposites, and the corpus says so: Spanish drops yo because the verb carries the person, Malayalam must keep njaan because the verb carries nothing.

points.label: second person: nii and ningal, and the respect the plural carries
points.note: The tu/usted question, answered with Malayalam's own machinery: respect is the plural, not a separate word.

points.label: third person: avan, aval, athu -- he, she, it
points.note: Not taught. The i-/a- deixis lesson gives ith and ath for THINGS, and aar ('who') for asking, but no third-person pronoun for a PERSON exists anywhere in the corpus. So a learner can say 'I' and 'you' and cannot say 'he' -- which also blocks every reported statement.

points.label: first and second person plural: njangal, naam, ningal
points.note: Only ningal is taught, and it is taught as respectful singular rather than as a plural. No word for 'we' exists, which is a large hole for a level whose functions include invitations and proposals.

points.label: the dative subject: enikku, where the experiencer is not the subject
points.note: Malayalam's answer to gustar, and a deeper one: knowing, liking and being hungry all happen TO you, so the person takes -ikku and the thing is the subject. Three Spanish points about indirect objects and gustar land here because this one construction is how Malayalam carries all of them.

points.label: interrogative pronouns: entu, aar
reflexive: doing something to oneself
points.note: No reflexive is taught. Malayalam uses thanne and a self-word; neither appears.

points.label: the relative participle, which is Malayalam's answer to relative que
points.note: UNTAUGHT, AND STRUCTURALLY THE BIGGEST GAP IN THIS FILE. Malayalam does not join with a relative pronoun at all: it turns the verb into a participle and puts the whole clause in front of the noun. Nothing in 292 lessons teaches it, so a learner cannot say 'the man who came'. Three Spanish points depend on it and all three are open.

points.label: exclamative: how good!, what a thing!
points.note: Not taught. enthoru and the exclamative use of the e- series are both absent.

points.label: the genitive: enre, 'my'
points.note: Taught as one word in chapter 2 rather than as a suffix, which is enough to say 'my name' and not enough to build a second possessor.

points.label: the genitive suffix itself: -nre / -ude on any noun
points.note: enre and ninre are both taught whole, and the suffix inside them is never named. So the learner owns two possessives and cannot make a third -- 'the teacher's book' is out of reach although both nouns are taught.

points.label: possession of a thing: 'I have', built with the dative and undu
points.note: Malayalam has no verb 'to have': undu plus a dative person is the whole construction, and both halves are taught. Restated around the Malayalam machinery.

points.label: cardinals one to five
cardinals six to ten
cardinals eleven to twenty, and the additive pattern behind them
points.note: The lesson teaches the pattern, not only the ten words, which is what makes it carry the general notion of number as well.

points.label: counting past twenty, and the hundreds
points.note: The count stops at twenty. Prices, ages over twenty and years are all out of reach.

points.label: ordinals: first, second, third
points.note: No ordinal is taught, so neither the ordering notion nor 'the first street on the left' is available.

points.label: relative quantity: more, less, a little
points.note: koodutal, kuravu and kurachu are chapter 58, and they answer the quantity question as short replies rather than as modifiers.

points.label: sufficiency: enough, that will do, no need
points.note: mathi, venda and athu mathi. A genuinely Malayalam cluster: the language answers 'do you want more?' with a single word far more often than Spanish does.

points.label: measures: size, distance and weight
points.note: valiya and cheriya give size as a quality. No unit of measure, no word for distance or weight, is taught.

points.label: the Malayalam numerals as written signs
points.note: Chapter 7's writing lessons teach the indigenous digit shapes, which the printed language now mostly replaces with the international ones -- but the track teaches them and they are enumerated here as taught.

points.label: the dative -ikku: to, for, and the person something happens to
points.note: Malayalam's most load-bearing suffix, and the corpus teaches the stacking idea with it. Spanish carries the same load with a plus a stressed pronoun.

points.label: the locative -il: in, at
points.note: Taught inside taamasikkuka, which is where a learner first needs it: 'I live IN somewhere'.

points.label: case suffixes stack onto the noun rather than standing in front of it
points.note: The typological fact a Spanish speaker most needs told: Malayalam glues where Spanish puts a separate word in front.

points.label: the accusative -e, and marking a human object
points.note: Not taught. Spanish marks a human direct object with a and can replace it with an unstressed clitic; Malayalam has no clitic object pronoun at all -- the object stays a full noun and takes -e. Neither the suffix nor the animacy rule appears anywhere, so both Spanish points are open on one missing suffix.

points.label: the instrumental and sociative: with, by means of
points.note: Neither -aal nor oppam is taught, so 'with a friend' and 'by bus' are both out of reach although suhruthu is taught.

points.label: the ablative -il ninnu: from a place
points.note: Not taught. Combined with the missing place names at ML-A1-N-02, 'where are you from' cannot be answered at all.

points.label: spatial postpositions: on, under, behind, in front of
points.note: None of mukalil, thaazhe, pinnil or munnil is taught. The track teaches five house objects and no way to say where any of them is.

points.label: the dictionary form in -uka, which is where every verb is looked up
points.note: Malayalam's citation form, and the form the corpus consistently heads its verb lessons with. It also carries the two Spanish infinitive-clause points, because the -uka form is what fills those slots.

points.label: the verb never agrees with its subject, in any person or number
points.note: The single largest simplification Malayalam offers, and the reason the pronoun cannot be dropped. Where Spanish spends fourteen verb points on paradigms, Malayalam spends one point saying there is no paradigm.

points.label: the present tense, one ending for everybody
points.note: pokuka's lesson is explicit that each of the three tense endings IS the entire conjugation.

points.label: the past tense, and the one place a Malayalam verb can still surprise you
points.note: Four Spanish past-tense points collapse into one, because Malayalam has one past and it is regular except in the stem. varuka is where the corpus teaches the irregularity.

points.label: the future tense
points.note: The third of pokuka's three endings, and the form plans and intentions are stated in.

points.label: the copula aanu: X is Y
points.note: Spanish spends five points on ser/estar and their attributes; Malayalam has one copula, it never agrees, and there is no second one to choose between. Five Spanish points, one Malayalam point.

points.label: undu: there is, there are, and having something
points.note: Malayalam's existential, doing the work of Spanish hay and tener at once. The same lesson teaches irikkuka, 'to be somewhere', which is the locational half.

points.label: the imperative in -oo, for a direct instruction
points.note: Chapters 43 and 44 teach eight imperatives as headwords -- nokku, kelkku, samsaarikku, ezhuthu -- which is the form itself taught eight times.

points.label: more imperatives: give, run, stand, sleep
points.note: The other four, and the ones that also carry the Spanish point about actions and positions of the body.

points.label: the -aam form: I'll do it, shall we, it may be
points.note: Taught inside the goodbye poyi varaam, and the corpus names the form. It is Malayalam's volitional-and-permissive, which is how offers, invitations and 'that would be all right' are all said.

points.label: the -anam form: should, must, please do
points.note: Taught inside kshamikkanam, 'you should forgive' -- which is how Malayalam apologises and also how it makes a softened request.

points.label: a noun plus ceyyuka, the way Malayalam makes new verbs
points.note: joli ceyyuka, 'work-do'. Productive, and worth a point because it is how a learner turns any of the track's many Sanskrit nouns into something they can do.

points.label: verbs of motion: to go and to come
verbs of perception: to see, to hear
verbs of the mind: to know, to think, to understand
verbs of the page: to read, to write
verbs of exchange: to ask, to take, to help
verbs of everyday living: to eat, to live somewhere, to speak
the present perfect: I have done it
points.note: Not taught. Malayalam builds it with the past participle plus undu, and neither the participle nor the construction appears -- so three Spanish points about participles and the perfect are open together.

points.label: the progressive: I am doing it right now
points.note: Not taught. The -kkunnu form is used inside ML-C05's sentence but never named as a form, and there is no gerund lesson.

points.label: the habitual past: I used to do it
points.note: Not taught, and correctly low priority: Malayalam has no separate imperfect, so the Spanish distinction has no Malayalam form to land on. Recorded because the SENSE still has to be sayable at A1.

points.label: ability: I can do it
points.note: kazhiyum and the -aan kazhiyum frame are not taught. Three Spanish points about ability and competence are open on one missing form.

points.label: wanting: I want
points.note: venam ('want, need') is not taught, although venda ('no need') is -- so the learner can refuse and cannot ask. That asymmetry is the single cheapest fix in this file.

points.label: illa: the existential negative, and the everyday 'no'
points.note: Malayalam's first negative and the one a beginner needs most.

points.label: alla: negating an identity rather than an existence
points.note: Malayalam splits its negation two ways -- illa denies that something IS THERE, alla denies that something IS SO. Only illa is taught, so 'I am not a teacher' cannot be said.

points.label: negative coordination: neither this nor that
points.note: Untaught, and it depends on the missing coordinator at ML-A1-JOIN-01.

points.label: refusing: no need, no thank you
points.note: venda, chapter 58. It is the polite refusal and the refusal of permission at once, which is how Malayalam actually works.

points.label: it does not matter, never mind
points.note: saaramilla, which is both the reply to an apology and Malayalam's 'you're welcome'.

points.label: the yes-or-no question particle -o, added to the end
points.note: Malayalam asks by adding one syllable and changing nothing else -- no inversion, no auxiliary. Worth a point of its own because it is so much cheaper than the Spanish machinery it replaces.

points.label: entu: what
aar: who
evide: where
engane: how
eppol: when
points.note: Not taught. The e- deixis lesson gives the pattern that would predict it, and the word itself never arrives -- so a learner who owns the days of the week cannot ask which one.

points.label: enthukondu: why
points.note: Neither the question word nor the because-word is taught, so cause cannot be asked about or given. See ML-A1-JOIN-05.

points.label: ethra: how much, how many
points.note: Taught inside the age question, which is the one place a beginner needs a quantity word.

points.label: asking for confirmation: a tag question
points.note: alle is not taught. The -o particle asks a genuine question; a tag question invites agreement, and Malayalam has a separate form for it.

points.label: confirming or denying what was just said
points.note: athe, illa and sari. The corpus teaches all three in chapter 1, which is why agreement and conformity are covered this early.

points.label: place: here and there
time: now, and the day after tomorrow
points.note: ippol and matrannaal. 'Today' and 'yesterday' are not taught -- see ML-A1-TIME-05.

points.label: manner: that way, just so
points.note: angane. bhangiyaayi ('well') and mosham ('badly') are not taught, so manner is answerable and not describable.

points.label: polarity: yes and no as one-word answers
sequence: then, soon, sometimes
points.note: pinne, udane, chilappol -- chapter 64. These order EVENTS across turns; they do not join clauses, which is the distinction ML-A1-JOIN-01 turns on.

points.label: restriction: only, that much and no more
points.note: maathram. tambien and tampoco have no taught Malayalam counterpart -- kooti is not taught -- so this point carries the restrictive half only.

points.label: certainty and doubt as adverbs: certainly, perhaps
points.note: theerchayaayum and orupakshe. Chapter 49 gives Malayalam a modal vocabulary before it has any modal verbs, which is an unusual shape and worth recording.

points.label: degree: very, quite, a bit
points.note: valare is not taught. Same gap as ML-A1-ADJ-05, from the adverb's side.

points.label: near and far, and how far away something is
points.note: aduthu and akale are not taught. ivide and avide give a two-way here/there and no way to say that something is FAR, so distance can be pointed at and not measured.

points.label: subject-object-verb: the verb comes last
points.note: njaan malayaalam samsaarikkunnu, and the word order it demonstrates. The reverse of Spanish, and the first thing a learner has to re-wire.

points.label: the copular sentence: X aanu Y
the existential sentence: undu with no subject at all
the dative-subject sentence, where the person is not the grammatical subject
points.note: enikku malayaalam ariyaam. The sentence type Spanish reaches with gustar, and Malayalam uses for knowing, liking, wanting and every bodily state.

points.label: the declarative, affirmative and negative
the yes-or-no question, and the wh-question
the vocative: calling somebody by name or role
points.note: No vocative particle and no term of address is taught. chettaa, chechi and the -e vocative are all absent, so a learner cannot open a conversation by addressing anyone.

points.label: the noun phrase: adjective plus noun, and nothing else
points.note: Adjective and demonstrative both precede, both invariable. The de-phrase and the relative clause, which the Spanish point also names, are ML-A1-POS-02 and ML-A1-PRON-08 and both are open.

points.label: and: joining two nouns, and joining two clauses
points.note: EMPTY, AND THIS IS THE HEADLINE FINDING. Malayalam's 'and' is the clitic -um, repeated on each item. It is not taught anywhere in 292 lessons. A learner who owns 66 chapters of vocabulary -- five body parts, five animals, five kitchen words -- cannot say 'rice and water'.

points.label: or: offering two alternatives
points.note: athava and allengil are both absent. So the Spanish function 'ask about a preference by offering alternatives' has no form to be asked in.

points.label: but: setting one thing against another
points.note: ennaal, chapter 64 -- the ONE point in this column that is covered, and the only clause connective the track teaches. It also carries the Spanish function 'offer a counter-argument with pero'.

points.label: distributive: one thing, then the other
points.note: Untaught, and dependent on the missing coordinator.

points.label: because: giving a reason
points.note: enthukondennaal and kaaranam are both absent. Combined with the missing 'why' at ML-A1-Q-07, cause cannot be asked for or supplied in either direction.

points.label: that-clauses: saying what somebody said or thinks
points.note: The quotative ennu is Malayalam's single most productive subordinator -- it turns any sentence into the object of 'say', 'think', 'know' or 'ask'. It is not taught. The track teaches cintikkuka, ariyuka and codikkuka and gives none of them anything to take as an object.

points.label: when: locating one event against another
points.note: The -mbol form is not taught, and neither is the question word eppol.

points.label: if: the conditional clause
points.note: The -aal conditional is not taught. Recorded separately from 'when' because Malayalam builds them with different suffixes.

points.label: in order to: purpose
points.note: The -aan purpose form is not taught, which also blocks the ability frame at ML-A1-V-22 -- both are built on it.

points.label: the relative participle: joining a clause to a noun
points.note: See ML-A1-PRON-08. Enumerated here as well because the Spanish inventory files it under subordination and this file must answer both.

points.label: the -i participle: doing one thing and then the next
points.note: poyi varaam -- 'having gone, I'll come'. Malayalam's real everyday clause-joiner IS this participle, and the corpus teaches it once, inside the goodbye, without naming it. That is the closest the track comes to teaching clause-joining, and it is why this column reads 2 of 11 rather than 1.

points.label: the days of the week
the months of the Kollam Era calendar
points.note: The track teaches the Malayalam solar calendar rather than the Gregorian months, which is a deliberate editorial choice and a genuine one -- but it means a learner cannot name the month on a form.

points.label: the seasons
the parts of the day: morning, noon, afternoon, evening, night, midnight
points.note: Six words across six chapters, which is unusually complete: this is the track's strongest column.

points.label: today, yesterday, tomorrow
points.note: innu and innale are NOT taught. naale ('tomorrow') appears only inside the fixed farewell naale kaanaam and is never taught as a word, so the learner has one third of the set and cannot use it apart from that phrase.

points.label: telling the clock time
points.note: mani plus a number, and the numbers reach twenty, so every hour is sayable.

points.label: the day itself: divasam, and the native naal beside it
asking and giving an age
points.note: ningalkku ethra vayassundu -- a dative subject plus the existential, which is a genuinely different shape from Spanish tener. The numbers stop at twenty, so an adult cannot answer it.

points.label: anteriority and posteriority: before and after
points.note: munpu and shesham are not taught. pinne ('then') is the nearest and it sequences turns rather than events.

points.label: locating an event in time: it is on Monday, it is at three
points.note: Requires the locative on a time word, which is not taught. The parts are all present -- days, hours, the -il suffix -- and are never assembled.

points.label: greet, in the way that works at any hour
greet by the time of day: good morning, good evening, good night, good afternoon
points.note: Four chapters, four formal Sanskrit-tatsama greetings. Their register is the subject of ML-A1-REG-01.

points.label: respond to a greeting
introduce oneself by name
ask somebody their name
respond to an introduction
points.note: santosham, 'joy' -- which is the whole reply.

points.label: ask how somebody is
thank
thank in the fuller register: gratitude, a favour, a blessing
points.note: Chapter 51 gives the noun vocabulary around thanking, which is how Malayalam says more than nandi.

points.label: reply to thanks
apologise
say please, and soften a request
give an order or instruction
ask for help
points.note: The verb is taught; the request frame that would turn it into 'can you help me' is not -- see ML-A1-V-22.

points.label: respond to a request: all right, that will do
ask for permission, and grant or refuse it
points.note: anuvaadam, sammatam and venda. Chapter 65 gives the nouns; the verb form that asks for permission is the missing -aamo, so this is covered as vocabulary and not as a frame.

points.label: make a request politely, and name what a request is
points.note: apeksha and maryaada -- chapter 65 is unusual in teaching the METALANGUAGE of politeness alongside the forms.

points.label: take leave
points.note: poyi varaam, and vida. The corpus is explicit that Malayalam does not say 'goodbye' but 'I will go and come back'.

points.label: arrange to meet again
say that one is setting off
welcome a guest
points.note: vaathil, kasera and athithi. The objects and the role are taught; the invitation frame is not.

points.label: express agreement
express disagreement
points.note: Covered only by the bare negative. Without alla (ML-A1-NEG-02) a learner can deny that something exists and cannot deny that something is so, which is what disagreement usually needs.

points.label: assert something as true, and as certain
hedge: perhaps, I am not sure
points.note: orupakshe. 'I don't know' as a frame needs the quotative and is not sayable -- see ML-A1-JOIN-06.

points.label: say that one knows, or does not know, something
points.note: enikku ... ariyaam is taught whole, and ariyuka is taught as a verb. Its negative ariyilla is not taught, so 'I do not know' is out of reach -- one of the three Spanish points here is only half answered and is recorded as covered because the frame and the verb both exist.

points.label: express what one likes
points.note: enikku ... ishtamaanu. A noun plus the copula plus a dative person, which is Malayalam's gustar and is taught as a whole construction.

points.label: give an opinion or an evaluation
points.note: OPEN, AND IT IS THE QUOTATIVE AGAIN. 'I think that ...' needs ennu plus cintikkuka; both halves of the evaluation vocabulary -- nallathu, moshamaanu -- are also absent. Five Spanish functional points sit on this one gap, which makes it the single highest-value fix in the file after the coordinator.

points.label: show one is following: I see, right, go on
state a plan or intention
points.note: The future ending and the -aam volitional between them carry intention, though no lesson frames them as such.

points.label: express a wish or a preference
points.note: venam is not taught -- see ML-A1-V-23.

points.label: ask somebody to be quiet
points.note: Not taught. The imperative set of chapters 43 and 44 does not include a quieting verb.

points.label: ask for a person: is X there?
points.note: Requires undu with a name and a question particle. Both parts are taught, the assembly is not, and there is no third-person pronoun (ML-A1-PRON-03) to refer to the person once found.

points.label: congratulate, toast, offer condolences
points.note: None of abhinandanangal, a toast formula, or a condolence formula is taught. Three Spanish social functions, one gap.

points.label: address somebody by name or title
points.note: See ML-A1-S-07: no term of address exists in the corpus.

points.label: accept or decline an offer
points.note: sari accepts, venda declines. Both are single words, which is how Malayalam actually does it.

points.label: say how one feels physically
points.note: vishappu, ksheenam and vedana -- and chapter 63's frame is the dative subject, so 'I am hungry' is enikku vishappundu.

points.label: greet and open a conversation at a door
express trust, respect and good manners as things one can name
points.note: vishvaasam, bahumaanam, maryaada. The track teaches the vocabulary of character before it teaches any character adjective.

points.label: the body: head and hand
the face: eye, ear, nose, mouth
the limbs: leg, tooth, hair, finger, stomach
the frame: neck, back, lip, nail, bone
the heart and the chest
physical characteristics of a person: tall, short, thin
points.note: Only valiya and cheriya are taught, and they describe things. No word for a person's build or height.

points.label: the immediate family: father, mother, and four age-graded siblings
points.note: Malayalam grades siblings by age rather than only by sex, so the six words are not the Spanish four.

points.label: children: child, son, daughter
grandparents and the married pair
family as a word, and friend
social roles: teacher, student, doctor, farmer, guest
food staples: water, raw rice, cooked rice
drinks: tea, coffee, milk
the meal itself
points.note: oon, and the second eat-verb behind it. The Spanish points also ask for the names of the meals of the day, which are not taught.

points.label: the kitchen shelf: coconut, oil, curd, jaggery, chilli
things you ask for: fruit, cloth, lamp, salt, book
the house: door, chair, mat, basket, box
points.note: Objects, yes; the names of the ROOMS of a dwelling, which the Spanish point also asks for, are not taught.

points.label: household tools: knife, vessel, rope, thread, needle, broom
colours: black, white, red, blue, green, yellow
animals of the house and the yard
the sky: sky, sun, moon, star, sunshine
the tree, part by part
the ground: river, rock, homeland, path, field
what the air carries: wind, sand, mud, smoke, ember
the weather as a word
points.note: kaalaavastha, 'the state of time'. The word for weather is taught and no weather adjective is, so a learner can name the topic and say nothing about it.

points.label: the paddy field: paddy, grass, ear of grain, plough, harvest
points.note: The track's economy vocabulary is agricultural, which is an editorial choice about Kerala and is recorded as one. It does not answer the Spanish industry point, which is about factories and energy.

points.label: illness: hunger, tiredness, pain, cough, fever
the doorway and its welcome: kolam, flower, garland
points.note: The nearest the track comes to the Spanish point about celebrations and occasions, and a genuinely Kerala answer to it.

points.label: clothing, footwear and accessories
points.note: thuni ('cloth') is the only textile word taught. Not one garment is named.

points.label: money, price and paying
points.note: No word for money, price, buying or selling appears anywhere. Three Spanish points, one gap, and it blocks the whole shopping scenario.

points.label: shops, and the people in them
points.note: kada is not taught. With ML-A1-LEX-30 this makes shopping unreachable in a track that teaches five kinds of vegetable oil's neighbours.

points.label: school and the classroom
points.note: Teacher, student and book. The institution, the timetable and classroom language are not taught, so four of the seven Spanish education points are open at ML-A1-LEX-33.

points.label: the education system: school, lesson, exam, marks
points.note: None of paLLikkoodam, paadam or pareeksha is taught.

points.label: learning and teaching as activities
work as an activity
conditions of work: rights, unemployment, what makes a good worker
points.note: Nothing in the corpus. Correctly low priority at A1 and recorded so the walk is total.

points.label: free time, sport, games, shows
points.note: Not one leisure word is taught in 292 lessons. Four Spanish points, one gap, and it is a large one for a level whose functions include invitations.

points.label: the telephone, the post, the internet, an e-mail address
points.note: Nothing. The Spanish inventory expects an A1 candidate to dictate an e-mail address; this track cannot name a telephone.

points.label: press, television and radio
points.note: Nothing taught.

points.label: housing as a transaction: buying, selling, renting
points.note: Nothing taught.

points.label: banks, health services, the police
points.note: vaidyan ('a doctor') is the only word in this whole area.

points.label: medicine, treatment and hygiene
points.note: The symptoms are taught (ML-A1-LEX-27) and nothing that treats them is.

points.label: travel, accommodation and transport
points.note: yaathra ('a journey') and vazhi ('a path') are the whole of it. No vehicle, no ticket, no place to stay -- so this is recorded as covered for the NOTION of a journey and the three Spanish points behind it remain thin.

points.label: documents: passport, identity card, personal data
points.note: Nothing taught. Name and age are available (ML-A1-F-04, ML-A1-TIME-08); address and telephone are not.

points.label: government, politics, law
points.note: Nothing taught, and correctly outside A1.

points.label: computing and technology
points.note: Nothing taught.

points.label: the arts: music, dance, literature, cinema
points.note: Nothing taught -- six Spanish points on one gap. Notable for a track whose culture is unusually rich here.

points.label: religion
points.note: anugraham ('a blessing') and maala ('a garland'). Thin, and genuinely present.

points.label: business and organisations
points.note: Nothing taught.

points.label: geography: country, town, city, capital
points.note: naadu ('home country') only -- see ML-A1-N-02.

points.label: open and closed, way in and way out
points.note: The door is taught and neither opening nor closing it is.

points.label: attractiveness: beautiful, ugly
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: good and bad as evaluations
points.note: nalla is taught and there is no word for bad, so evaluation runs one way only. Three Spanish points depend on the pair and are half answered by half of it.

points.label: ease and difficulty
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: eating out: the restaurant, ordering, the bill
points.note: Nothing taught. The track teaches the meal at home -- oon, rice, curd, jaggery -- and no word for a place that serves one. With the missing money vocabulary at ML-A1-LEX-30 the whole restaurant scenario is closed.

points.label: the script is an abugida: a consonant carries an inherent vowel until a sign changes it
points.note: The chandrakkala, taught twice -- as a shape in chapter 1's writing arc and as a recognised sign at ML-S02. This is the fact that makes Malayalam readable at all, and Spanish's alphabet points are what it answers.

points.label: the independent vowel letters
points.note: a, aa, i, e, u, uu, oo as free-standing letters.

points.label: the dependent vowel signs that hang off a consonant
points.note: Ten matra signs, which is the part of the script a reader meets on every word.

points.label: the chillu letters: consonants that end a word without a vowel
points.note: Malayalam has a distinct set of word-final consonant shapes that no other Indic script keeps in this form, and four of the six are taught.

points.label: the anusvara, which closes so many Malayalam nouns
the everyday consonants: the first eight a beginner meets
the retroflex and the distinctively Dravidian consonants
points.note: nna, tta, the zha that Malayalam shares only with Tamil, and rra.

points.label: the Sanskrit-borrowed consonants a Malayalam text cannot do without
points.note: ssa, da, sa, ha, bha, tha, ga, ja. The track teaches a lot of Sanskrit vocabulary and these are the letters it is written with.

points.label: reading a whole known word back off the page
points.note: Chapter 1's arc ends by assembling namaskaram from shapes already met, which is the moment reading starts.

points.label: writing a known word from sound alone
points.note: The trace / guided-copy / delayed-copy / dictation ladder, which the track runs twice.

points.label: the indigenous Malayalam numerals
the nine characters the corpus uses in headwords and never teaches
points.note: MEASURED, NOT ESTIMATED. 67 distinct Malayalam characters appear in headwords across 292 lessons and 58 are taught by a script lesson -- 87 per cent closure, between Tamil's 52 of 52 and Kannada's 50 of 69. The nine open ones, by the number of headwords that need them: sha (14), lla (10), chillu-rr (8), nga (8), the ai sign (5), dha (5), ba (3), kha (3), cha (2). sha alone blocks fourteen taught words including sari, the first-chapter 'okay'.

points.label: capital letters
points.note: Malayalam has no case distinction, so the Spanish points have no Malayalam counterpart. Enumerated rather than dropped: a reader comparing the files should see the answer.

points.label: written accentuation
points.note: Malayalam has no accent marks. Same reasoning as ML-A1-SCR-13.

points.label: punctuation: the full stop, comma, question mark and the rest
points.note: Modern Malayalam uses the European marks, and not one lesson teaches any of them. Nine Spanish points on one gap. Cheap to close and entirely open.

points.label: abbreviations and initialisms
points.note: Nothing taught, and correctly marginal at A1.

points.label: the retroflex series, which English does not have
points.note: Taught as shapes rather than as sounds. Recorded as covered for the CONTRAST being present in the corpus at all, and it is fair to call that thin.

points.label: zha, the sound Malayalam shares only with Tamil
points.note: ML-C33-ezhutuka names it explicitly as the letter Tamil also carries, which is the one place the corpus teaches a sound as a sound.

points.label: long and short vowels as a meaning difference
points.note: The vowel signs are taught as shapes; no lesson says that length changes the word.

points.label: gemination: the doubled consonant
points.note: The chandrakkala is taught and the doubling it writes is never named as a contrast, although it appears in dozens of taught headwords.

points.label: word stress
points.note: Not taught anywhere. Malayalam's stress is regular, which is exactly why one lesson would settle it for good.

points.category: Bhaashaabhedam (register: Sanskritic and native, familiar and respectful)
points.label: the Sanskrit-tatsama greeting against the everyday one
points.note: MEASURED FROM THIS TRACK, NOT BORROWED FROM TAMIL. Four lessons in this corpus carry register: formal, and every one of them is a Sanskrit-tatsama time-of-day greeting; namaskaram is respectful-neutral and works at any hour. That is a lexical register split between borrowed and inherited words -- it is NOT Tamil's literary/spoken diglossia, and this file does not claim one.

points.category: Bhaashaabhedam (register: Sanskritic and native, familiar and respectful)
points.label: the native word narrowed into narrative or literary use
points.note: The only two lessons in the corpus marked register: literary-narrative and literary. Both teach a native word that the everyday Sanskrit one displaced -- naal beside divasam, iravu beside raathri. A learner needs to recognise them and should not produce them, and the corpus marks that.

points.category: Bhaashaabhedam (register: Sanskritic and native, familiar and respectful)
points.label: respect expressed as plurality: nii against ningal
points.note: The one register distinction a beginner must produce correctly from the first conversation.

points.category: Bhaashaabhedam (register: Sanskritic and native, familiar and respectful)
points.label: the politeness vocabulary as a thing that can be named
points.note: maryaada and bahumaanam. Unusual: the track hands the learner the words FOR politeness before it hands them many polite forms.

points.category: Bhaashaabhedam (register: Sanskritic and native, familiar and respectful)
points.label: when to use the formal greeting and when the everyday one
points.note: The corpus teaches four formal greetings and namaskaram and never states the rule for choosing between them. The evidence is in the lessons' own register fields; the guidance is not in their prose.
